source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing (cut thinking off, or append Wait to extend it) gives a controllable accuracy-versus-thinking-tokens curve for a model tuned on 1,000 examples.
numbers: s1-32B AIME24 50% without intervention to 57% with Wait appended; Wait forced 2, 4, 6 times in Fig 4; control 100%, scaling slope 15, AIME24 56.7 in Table 3.
limits: Curve flattens or hits context limits at the top; one model family; AIME24 has only 30 questions so 1 question is 3.3 points.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a forced-stop quality curve exists for LLMs. Supports a hard compute cap (G6) with a stop rule.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1 ablation: prompting the model with a token limit
finding: Telling the model how many tokens to use in the prompt does not control length. Hard truncation does.
numbers: Token-conditional control alone: control 40% (2 of 5 runs under limit), scaling slope -24. With truncation added: control 100% (5 of 5), slope 13. Step-conditional prompting also tested.
limits: AIME24 only, small model, n=5 runs per setting.
agent_relevance: A scaffold cannot trust the model to self-limit; enforce budgets outside the model (G12 style external stop).

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1 ablation: parallel sampling versus sequential extension
finding: Majority voting over 2 to 64 samples of Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct was compared with sequential Wait extension; sequential extrapolated better in their setup.
numbers: 64 evaluations per question at temperature 1, majority vote at 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64; rejection sampling to hit a length cap needed 655 tries per sample at the tightest cap and 1 at the loosest.
limits: Different base models in the two arms; rival finding in Ghosal et al. (b04).
agent_relevance: Two ways to spend time: longer chain or more chains. Needs a choice rule.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling
finding: Extending thinking with Wait gives first a gain and then a decline across models and benchmarks. A simple model says extra thinking raises output variance, which looks like gain at first.
numbers: With a fixed 16K token budget, parallel thinking with majority vote gives about 22% higher accuracy than Wait-and-think-more and about 47% higher than exact-thinking budget control.
limits: The probabilistic model is a toy. Comparison to s1 uses different models and metrics.
agent_relevance: Prefer several short independent attempts plus a vote over one long chain when budget is fixed.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR)
finding: On some tasks, longer reasoning lowers accuracy. Five failure modes: distraction, framing overfit, spurious correlation, lost focus on deduction, more self-preservation talk.
numbers: Misleading Python distractors: Claude Opus 4 accuracy drops from near-perfect to about 80% with extended reasoning; o3 scales positively; R1 flat. Grades regression: inverse scaling in Sonnet 3.7, Opus 4, o3-mini (controlled), mixed or flat in others.
limits: Effects are model-specific and setup-specific (controlled versus natural overthinking). Natural overthinking gives noisier patterns. Tasks were built to elicit the effect.
agent_relevance: Anytime quality is not monotone for LLMs. G6 should include a stop on non-improvement, and answers should be kept from the best point, not the last.

source: Gema et al. (2025) inverse scaling, Misleading Math with well-known framing
finding: Models that recognize a familiar puzzle framing apply memorized solutions as reasoning gets longer.
numbers: Claude Opus 4 and DeepSeek R1 show inverse scaling in controlled overthinking; o-series resists distractors but overfits framing.
limits: Specific to constructed tasks.
agent_relevance: Long reasoning can amplify a wrong prior; require evidence checks.

source: Su et al. (2025) Between Underthinking and Overthinking
finding: Models overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones: they do not scale length to difficulty. Preferring shorter outputs cut length with acceptable accuracy loss.
numbers: Correct answers tend to be shorter at the per-question level (length-ranked analysis, Fig 1). Exact per-model deltas not extracted.
limits: Length is a signal, not a cause.
agent_relevance: Metareasoning gap: the model misjudges difficulty. The scaffold needs an external difficulty or progress estimate.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend many tokens on easy items, and most later reasoning rounds add nothing. The first solution round is usually already right.
numbers: In more than 92% of cases the first round of solutions is correct; first round is under 60% of tokens; ASDIV first round 287 tokens, 38.7% of response; SimPO cut tokens 22.3% on MATH500.
limits: Mostly QwQ-32B-Preview; first-answer trimming hurt on MATH500, the hard set.
agent_relevance: Cheap early answer plus verification beats a long chain on easy items. Supports early exit and anytime answers.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Overthinking, length-reduction methods
finding: Keeping only the first correct solution cuts the most tokens but hurts the hard test set; adding reflection restores some accuracy.
numbers: First-Correction-Solutions gives the biggest cut; drop on MATH500; FCS+Reflection recovers part.
limits: Self-training on one model; no exact deltas extracted.
agent_relevance: Quality curve is difficulty-dependent: trim only when the item is easy.

source: Wu et al. (2025) When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
finding: Accuracy follows an inverted U with chain-of-thought length. Optimal length rises with task difficulty and falls with model capability.
numbers: Optimal length fell from 14 steps (1.5B) to 4 steps (72B); difficulty correlated with optimal length, p about 1e-8; gap between optimal and longest length up to 40% accuracy for the 72B model.
limits: Small question samples (30 per model, 100 for difficulty); theory is a simple model.
agent_relevance: Fixes the shape of the curve for LLMs: peak then decline, with the peak moving with difficulty. Argues for adaptive stopping.

source: Wu et al. (2025) When More is Less: RL training shortens chains
finding: RL training gravitates toward shorter chains as accuracy improves, matching a simplicity bias.
numbers: Replicated in a synthetic GPT-2 experiment.
limits: Synthetic setup; theory-driven.
agent_relevance: Supports early commit when the model is strong.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: On puzzles with controlled complexity, reasoning models beat plain models only at medium complexity. At high complexity both collapse, and reasoning effort falls although tokens remain.
numbers: Three regimes: low complexity plain models better; medium reasoning models better; high both collapse to zero. Effort rises then declines with complexity.
limits: Contested by b13. Token output limits and impossible instances may explain part of the collapse.
agent_relevance: The quality curve depends on problem complexity; a stop rule must handle both ends.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking
finding: Comment arguing the collapse is an artifact: Tower of Hanoi outputs hit token limits, and some River Crossing instances (N of 6 or more) are mathematically impossible but scored as failures.
numbers: With a request for a generating function instead of a move list, preliminary runs show high accuracy on Hanoi sizes reported as failures. No large table given.
limits: Preliminary short comment; not peer reviewed at time of reading.
agent_relevance: Warning: truncation at a budget can look like reasoning failure. Log why a run stopped.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally
finding: The best way to spend test-time compute depends on prompt difficulty. Allocating per prompt beats a fixed best-of-N.
numbers: More than 4x efficiency gain over best-of-N; a smaller model with test-time compute beats a 14x larger model on easy and medium prompts; on hard prompts or high inference load, pretraining wins. Beam search better on hard questions and low budgets, best-of-N on easy questions and high budgets.
limits: MATH with PaLM 2; difficulty bins come from the model's own pass rate, which has a cost; one benchmark family.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for allocating compute by difficulty (G6). The difficulty estimate has a cost that must be paid.

source: Snell et al. (2024) sequential versus parallel ratio
finding: Easy questions do best with purely sequential revisions; hard ones do best with a balanced mix of sequential and parallel.
numbers: Generation budget 128 tested across difficulty bins; ideal ratio depends on budget and question.
limits: Revision model fine-tuned by the authors; MATH only.
agent_relevance: Choose between revise-in-place and sample-more based on difficulty.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys
finding: Coverage (any sample right) grows log-linearly over four orders of magnitude of samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples versus single-sample state of the art 43%. CodeContests Gemma-2B coverage 0.02% to 7.1%.
limits: Needs automatic verifiers for the gain to be realized.
agent_relevance: A verifier is what makes more time pay off. Without one, stop early.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys, verification plateau
finding: Without a verifier, voting and reward-model selection plateau beyond about 100 samples, opening a gap to the coverage upper bound.
numbers: Plateau near 100 samples while coverage keeps climbing.
limits: Math and open-ended domains tested; gap size varies.
agent_relevance: Selection quality, not generation, is the bottleneck of added time.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Inference Scaling Laws (ICLR)
finding: Small models with a good search strategy can be Pareto-optimal against bigger models at equal compute.
numbers: Llemma-7B with their tree search beats Llemma-34B across tested strategies on MATH.
limits: Math only; gains diminish at large compute.
agent_relevance: Compute-for-size trade is real but bounded; pick strategy by budget.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) L1: Controlling How Long a Reasoning Model Thinks (COLM)
finding: Training with length targets in the prompt gives precise control and a smooth accuracy-versus-length curve, beating s1 budget forcing at small budgets.
numbers: Versus s1 at 512 and 1024 tokens: over 100 to 150% relative and 20 to 25% absolute gain. Log-linear slope 0.24 versus 0.37 for s1. 1.5B L1 is 5% better than its non-reasoning base and 2% better than GPT-4o at equal short lengths.
limits: Needs RL training; our agent uses a scaffold only. 1.5B model, math focus.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level budgets work only if trained; a scaffold must enforce budgets externally.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) L1 transfer and cost
finding: Length control trained on math carries to logic and MMLU-style tasks; long-CoT models become good short-CoT models.
numbers: L1-Exact is about 1% below DeepScaleR-4K (same base, no length constraints).
limits: Small cost in peak accuracy.
agent_relevance: Budget conditioning costs little; capping time is cheap.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) L1 versus s1 as cross-check of hard truncation
finding: A second group compared against s1 budget forcing: s1 loses much accuracy at small budgets because truncation cuts reasoning mid-way.
numbers: 20 to 25 points absolute gap at 512 and 1024 tokens.
limits: Different base models, so not a clean replication.
agent_relevance: A hard cut at a small budget costs accuracy; plan to answer before the cap.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute
finding: Thinking offline before the query arrives shifts the time-quality trade.
numbers: Same accuracy with about 5x less test-time compute on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME; up to +13% and +18% accuracy when scaling sleep-time compute; 2.5x lower cost per query when amortized over related queries.
limits: Works when the query is predictable; benefit correlates with predictability. Benchmarks modified by the authors.
agent_relevance: Pre-compute during idle states; fits caching of derived facts.

source: Hay, Russell, Tolpin, Shimony (2012) Selecting Computations: Theory and Applications
finding: Metalevel selection of computations is a Bayesian selection problem, not a bandit. Bandit policies are biased away from low-estimate options and have no stopping rule. If the myopic policy computes, the optimal policy does too (Theorem 7); if myopic stops in a closed set of states, optimal stops (Theorem 9).
numbers: First finite sampling bounds for optimal policies in certain cases; includes a counterexample to an intuitive conjecture about optimal policies.
limits: Theory with simple models; myopic value of information can stop too soon when one step has no value.
agent_relevance: Gives a principled stop rule: stop when estimated gain per extra step falls below its cost. Warns against UCB-style spending.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think
finding: Frames the problem as choosing whether to think at all. Only the introduction was seen this session.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: No numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Supports a no-think-first gate for easy items.

source: Zilberstein (1996) Using Anytime Algorithms in Intelligent Systems
finding: Defines anytime algorithms and performance profiles: quality as a function of time, with properties such as measurable, recognizable, monotonic, consistent. Not opened this session (search quota used up).
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Pointer only, from background knowledge.
agent_relevance: Origin of the quality-versus-time curve concept.

source: Dean and Boddy (1988) An Analysis of Time-Dependent Planning
finding: Time-dependent planning and expected-value scheduling with performance profiles. Not opened this session.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Pointer only.
agent_relevance: Source of profile-based scheduling.

source: Russell and Wefald (1991) Principles of Metareasoning
finding: Value of computation as expected gain minus time cost; myopic greedy approximation. Not opened; the myopic rule is confirmed second-hand in b23.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Pointer only.
agent_relevance: Basis for a marginal-gain stop rule.

source: Simon (1955) A Behavioral Model of Rational Choice
finding: Satisficing: search until an option meets an aspiration level. Not opened this session.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Pointer only. Setting the aspiration level is the hard part.
agent_relevance: Cheap stop rule: accept the first answer above threshold and verified.
